{"body": "I have no earlier body for this node; the only committed material I actually see is a pointer to a source that is absent, plus the instruction to express uncertainty caused by the view I have. So I cannot honestly report what an earlier treatment concluded about black hole evaporation and its bearing on information about physical state. What I can state is the shape of the problem as it is usually posed, without treating that shape as a settled result.

In semi-classical gravity, a black hole formed by collapse is expected to radiate approximately thermally, with a temperature inversely proportional to its mass. If that radiation is exactly thermal and the hole disappears completely, then the post-evaporation state appears to be describable without reference to the details of what fell in. That apparent loss of dependence on the initial microstate is the tension usually called the black hole information problem.

The honest position here is conditional. The claim that information is destroyed depends on conjunctive assumptions: that the evaporation is complete; that the outgoing radiation is genuinely thermal or otherwise factorizes from the interior; that no subtle correlations, remnants, or non-unitary effects carry the dependence forward; and that the appropriate notion of information is the one used in the argument. Different proposals attack different conjuncts. The alternatives include: information escapes in subtle correlations in the Hawking radiation; the evaporation leaves a remnant that stores it; the process is not unitary and information is genuinely lost; or the question is malformed because the correct description is not the semi-classical one, so 'what happens to it' has no well-defined answer framed in those terms.

I can name those alternatives as positions, not as results I am endorsing. I do not have, in the material exposed here, a derivation, a measurement, or a prior node's conclusion that would adjudicate between them. The problem therefore remains open from this vantage: the physical answer depends on which of the above assumptions fails, and that has not been settled by anything I can see at this node.

A further uncertainty is terminological. 'Information about the physical state' can mean the full microstate, or a coarse-grained specification, or a set of conserved quantities. Whether anything is lost can depend on which is meant. I have not been given a source that fixes the intended sense.", "commitments": "Taking this up would commit me to treating the black hole information problem as conditional rather than solved: specifically, to the claim that the apparent loss of dependence on initial microstate rests on a conjunction of assumptions about completeness of evaporation, thermality or factorization of the radiation, absence of correlations or remnants, and the intended sense of information. It would also commit me to the weaker claim that I currently see no adjudicating material at this node, so I cannot assert which conjunct fails or that information is or is not destroyed.

What I am not committing to: I am not asserting that information is preserved, lost, or encoded in radiation, nor that any particular proposed resolution is correct. Naming the alternatives is a map of positions, not an endorsement of any of them.

What would need to be supplied to move past this: an earlier node's actual conclusion, a derivation or calculation showing how the outgoing state does or does not depend on the initial microstate, or a clarification of which sense of information is at issue. Without one of those, any stronger commitment on my part would be invention rather than uptake.

A useful test of this contribution is whether it correctly refuses to fill the absent source with a fabricated conclusion while still naming the structure of the problem. Its relevance is limited to the problem as posed; it does not test any specific resolution."}
